claim: ACAPseq is a novel platform for identifying protein-protein interactions (PPIs).
source: Here, we present a novel platform - Affinity Capture of Polyribosomes followed by RNA sequencing (ACAPseq) - for identifying PPIs.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that ACAPseq is a novel platform for identifying PPIs.

claim: ACAPseq harnesses massively parallel RNA sequencing to quantify enrichment of polyribosomes based on nascent polypeptide affinity for an immobilized protein bait.
source: ACAPseq harnesses the power of massively parallel RNA sequencing (RNAseq) to quantify the enrichment of polyribosomes based on the affinity of their associated nascent polypeptides for an immobilized protein 'bait'.
evidence: The abstract describes the mechanism by which ACAPseq operates.

claim: ACAPseq was developed and tested using neonatal mouse brain polyribosomes and various extracellular domains as baits.
source: This method was developed and tested using neonatal mouse brain polyribosomes and a variety of extracellular domains as baits.
evidence: The abstract describes the experimental system used to develop ACAPseq.

claim: Of 92 baits tested, 25 identified one or more biologically relevant binding partners.
source: Of 92 baits tested, 25 identified one or more binding partners that appear to be biologically relevant; additional candidate partners remain to be validated.
evidence: The abstract provides quantitative results from the ACAPseq experiments.

claim: ACAPseq can detect binding to targets present at less than 1 part in 100,000 in the starting polyribosome preparation.
source: ACAPseq can detect binding to targets that are present at less than 1 part in 100,000 in the starting polyribosome preparation.
evidence: The abstract states the sensitivity of the ACAPseq method.

claim: The mode of homophilic binding for Protocadherin-9 (PCDH9) was revealed through detailed analysis of one observed PPI.
source: One of the observed PPIs was analyzed in detail, revealing the mode of homophilic binding for Protocadherin-9 (PCDH9), a non-clustered Protocadherin family member.
evidence: The abstract describes a specific finding from the study.

claim: Mass spectrometry of purified protein complexes is limited to relatively high affinity interactions and by sample quantity and purity.
source: Mass spectrometry of purified protein complexes provides an unbiased approach to identifying PPIs, but it is limited to relatively high affinity interactions as well as by sample quantity and purity (Gavin et al., 2011; Frei et al., 2012).
evidence: The introduction cites published literature to support this limitation of mass spectrometry.

claim: Direct binding assays using immobilized fusion proteins require production, purification, and analysis of hundreds or thousands of proteins.
source: Direct binding assays using immobilized fusion proteins have high sensitivity but require production, purification, and analysis of hundreds or thousands of proteins (Bushell et al., 2008; Ramani et al., 2012; Özkan et al., 2013; Tom et al., 2015; Visser et al., 2015; Hsu et al., 2017).
evidence: The introduction cites published literature to support this characteristic of direct binding assays.

claim: Proximity labeling assays like BioID tag nearby proteins, but only a subset of these likely interact directly with the protein of interest.
source: Proximity labeling assays, such as BioID, tag nearby proteins but only a subset of these is likely to interact directly with the protein of interest (Fernández-Suárez et al., 2008; Roux et al., 2012; Schopp et al., 2017).
evidence: The introduction cites published literature to support this limitation of proximity labeling assays.

claim: Immuno-affinity capture of polyribosomes was developed by Schimke and colleagues as a method for purifying specific eukaryotic mRNAs.
source: This method was inspired by the work of Schimke and colleagues, who developed immuno-affinity capture of polyribosomes as a method for purifying specific eukaryotic mRNAs (Palmiter et al., 1972).
evidence: The introduction cites the original work that inspired ACAPseq.

claim: Immuno-affinity capture of polyribosomes was used to enrich several low abundance mRNAs to facilitate their cloning.
source: Immuno-affinity capture of polyribosomes was subsequently used to enrich several low abundance mRNAs to facilitate their cloning (Korman et al., 1982; Kraus and Rosenberg, 1982).
evidence: The introduction cites published literature describing applications of polyribosome capture.

claim: Affinity capture of polyribosomes followed by ribosome profiling has been used to interrogate interactions between nascent polypeptides and chaperones or targeting factors.
source: More recently, affinity capture of polyribosomes followed by ribosome profiling has been used to interrogate interactions between nascent polypeptides and chaperones or targeting factors, such as signal recognition particle (Schibich et al., 2016; Döring et al., 2017).
evidence: The introduction cites published literature describing recent applications of polyribosome capture.

claim: Ribosome display was developed as an in vitro approach for identifying high affinity interactions between libraries of mutant proteins and an immobilized ligand.
source: A further variation on this method, ribosome display, was developed as an in vitro approach for identifying high affinity interactions between libraries of mutant proteins and an immobilized ligand (Zahnd et al., 2007; Plückthun, 2012; Schilling et al., 2014).
evidence: The introduction cites published literature describing ribosome display.

claim: PLATO (parallel analysis of translated open reading frames) is a method adapted from ribosome display for discovering PPIs and protein-drug interactions.
source: The ribosome display technique has been further adapted by Zhu et al., 2013 for the discovery of PPIs and protein-drug interactions by in vitro transcription, translation, and ribosome capture starting from a normalized collection of human cDNAs, a method referred to as parallel analysis of translated open reading frames (PLATO).
evidence: The introduction cites published literature describing PLATO.

claim: ACAPseq is conceptually similar to PLATO.
source: ACAPseq is conceptually similar to PLATO.
evidence: The introduction explicitly states the relationship between ACAPseq and PLATO.

claim: Many extracellular proteins have biologically important interactions.
source: In developing ACAPseq, we focused on mammalian protein domains that reside in the extracellular space, because (1) many of these proteins have biologically important interactions
evidence: The introduction provides rationale for focusing on extracellular proteins.

claim: Many extracellular binding interactions involve domains that are likely to fold independently.
source: (2) many extracellular binding interactions involve domains that are likely to fold independently (e.g. cadherin, fibronectin, and Ig domains)
evidence: The introduction provides rationale for focusing on extracellular proteins.

claim: Most single-pass transmembrane proteins consist of an amino-terminal extracellular domain and a carboxy-terminal intracellular domain.
source: (3) most single-pass transmembrane proteins, including many cell surface receptors, consist of an amino-terminal extracellular domain (ECD) and a carboxy-terminal intracellular domain (ICD), the optimal arrangement of the ECD for a method that relies on binding in the context of a nascent polypeptide
evidence: The introduction describes the structural organization of transmembrane proteins.

claim: Most extracellular domains contain one or more disulfide bonds and generally do not fold properly in the reducing environment of the cytoplasm.
source: (4) most extracellular domains contain one or more disulfide bonds and, in general, these domains do not fold properly in the reducing environment of the cytoplasm and are therefore not amenable to yeast or mammalian two-hybrid approaches.
evidence: The introduction describes biochemical properties of extracellular domains.

claim: Poly-valent interactions between immobilized bait proteins and nascent polypeptides on a single polyribosome may enable ACAPseq to identify relatively weak interactions.
source: Moreover, the potential for poly-valent interactions between several immobilized bait proteins and several nascent polypeptides associated with a single polyribosome suggested that ACAPseq might be useful for identifying relatively weak interactions.
evidence: The introduction provides a hypothesis about ACAPseq's capability.

claim: Protein baits were produced as secreted human IgG1 Fc fusion proteins following transient transfection of HEK/293T cells.
source: Protein baits were produced as secreted human IgG1 Fc fusion proteins following transient transfection of mammalian (HEK/293T) cells, immobilized on the surface of Protein-G-coated magnetic beads, and used to capture polyribosomes prepared from neonatal mouse brain, a tissue that expresses a large and diverse set of genes (Figure 1A).
evidence: The Results section describes the experimental methodology, and Figure 1A illustrates the workflow.

claim: Baits were immobilized on Protein-G-coated magnetic beads.
source: Protein baits were produced as secreted human IgG1 Fc fusion proteins following transient transfection of mammalian (HEK/293T) cells, immobilized on the surface of Protein-G-coated magnetic beads, and used to capture polyribosomes prepared from neonatal mouse brain, a tissue that expresses a large and diverse set of genes (Figure 1A).
evidence: The Results section describes the experimental methodology, and Figure 1A illustrates the workflow.

claim: Polyribosomes were prepared from neonatal mouse brain.

claim: Capturing polyribosomes with multiple baits in parallel permitted comparison of capture efficiencies among different baits.

evidence: The Results section describes advantages of the parallel capture approach.

claim: Typical RNA yields from ACAPseq capture reactions were in the several nanogram range.
source: Typical RNA yields from ACAPseq capture reactions were in the several nanogram range.

claim: Approximately 10 million RNAseq reads per bait are sufficient for identification of captured mRNAs.
source: In our experience,~10 million RNAseq reads per bait are sufficient for identification of captured mRNAs.

claim: For Fc-VEGF with total brain polyribosomes as control and a fold-enrichment cut-off of three, the sensitivity is 1.0 with an FDR ranging from 0.9 to 0.95.

evidence: The Results section provides quantitative performance metrics shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: For Fc-VEGF with irrelevant baits as control and a fold-enrichment cut-off of three, the sensitivity is 0.75 with an FDR ranging from 0 to 0.69.
source: With irrelevant baits as the control, the sensitivity was 0.75 with an FDR ranging from 0 to 0.69.
evidence: The Results section provides quantitative performance metrics shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: For Fc-VEGF, the specificity varied from 0.987 to 1.0 across the parameter values explored.
source: Across the parameter values explored here, the specificity varied from 0.987 to 1.0.
evidence: The Results section provides quantitative performance metrics shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: For EFNA1-Fc, ACAPseq performance was relatively insensitive to the range of parameter values tested, with sensitivities of 0.89-1.0, specificities of 0.977-0.997, and FDRs of 0.64-0.93.
source: For EFNA1-Fc, ACAPseq performance was relatively insensitive to this range of parameter values, with sensitivities of 0.89 – 1.0 (for nine true EPH targets), specificities of 0.977 – 0.997, and FDRs of 0.64 – 0.93.
evidence: The Results section provides quantitative performance metrics shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: For EFNA1-Fc, the TPM cut-off could be set as high as 60 with little effect on sensitivity and specificity.
source: The TPM cut-off could be set as high as 60 with little effect on EFNA1-Fc sensitivity and specificity.
evidence: The Results section describes the robustness of EFNA1-Fc performance to parameter changes.

claim: No single set of cut-off parameters are optimal for all baits.
source: Taken together, these examples show the high performance of ACAPseq, but they also imply that no single set of cut-off parameters are optimal for all baits, presumably due to differences in the starting abundance of target mRNAs, the affinities of bait-target binding, and the abundance of mRNAs coding for targets that bind nonspecifically to the bait.
evidence: The Results section provides an interpretation of the performance analysis.

claim: A total of 1207 supra-threshold targets were found for the 92 baits using the defined threshold criteria.
source: With these criteria, we found a total of 1207 supra-threshold targets for the 92 baits (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: The Results section provides quantitative results from the screen.

claim: The distribution of targets per bait is highly skewed.
source: The distribution of targets per bait is highly skewed (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), with six baits showing >50 targets per bait and three baits showing >100 targets per bait, suggesting that the small fraction of baits that had a large number (e.g. >30) targets may be nonspecifically sticky.
evidence: The Results section describes the distribution of targets shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Six baits showed more than 50 targets per bait.
source: The distribution of targets per bait is highly skewed (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), with six baits showing >50 targets per bait and three baits showing >100 targets per bait
evidence: The Results section provides quantitative data on target distribution shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Three baits showed more than 100 targets per bait.
source: The distribution of targets per bait is highly skewed (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), with six baits showing >50 targets per bait and three baits showing >100 targets per bait
evidence: The Results section provides quantitative data on target distribution shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Baits with a large number of targets may be nonspecifically sticky.
source: suggesting that the small fraction of baits that had a large number (e.g. >30) targets may be nonspecifically sticky.
evidence: The Results section provides an interpretation of the target distribution data.

claim: Fifty-two baits (57%) showed 1-10 targets per bait.
source: Fifty-two baits (57%) showed 1 – 10 targets per bait and 15 baits (16%) showed no targets.
evidence: The Results section provides quantitative data on target distribution.

claim: Fifteen baits (16%) showed no targets.
source: Fifty-two baits (57%) showed 1 – 10 targets per bait and 15 baits (16%) showed no targets.
evidence: The Results section provides quantitative data on target distribution.

claim: Among 86 baits derived from different genes, 24 (28%) capture one or more biologically plausible targets.
source: Among the 86 baits derived from different genes, 24 (28%) capture one or more targets that (1) are biologically plausible (i.e. the target is an extracellular or transmembrane protein with large extracellular domains), (2) have an ACAPseq signal that is well in excess of non-specific binding, and (3) are experimentally validated in the present study, were previously reported, and/or are related to a previously reported target (e.g. is a member of the same protein family) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The Results section provides quantitative data on validated targets.

claim: There were 64 bait-target pairs that are biologically plausible, have high ACAPseq signal, and are validated or related to previously reported targets.
source: Altogether, there were 64 bait-target pairs in this category.
evidence: The Results section provides quantitative data on validated targets.

claim: There is a surprisingly low degree of overlap between ACAPseq and BioGRID candidate PPIs.
source: A comparison of ACAPseq with two large public data bases of PPIs – BioGRID (Stark et al., 2006; http://www.thebiogrid.org) and IntAct (Orchard et al., 2014; https://www.ebi.ac.uk/intact/) - show a surprisingly low degree of overlap among candidate PPIs.
evidence: The Results section compares ACAPseq results with existing databases.

claim: There were only eight bait-target pairs in common between BioGRID and the ACAPseq dataset.
source: Among baits that were listed in these databases and tested in the present study (47 for BioGRID and 43 for IntAct), there were only eight bait-target pairs in common between each database and the ACAPseq dataset (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The Results section provides quantitative comparison with BioGRID shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claim: There were only eight bait-target pairs in common between IntAct and the ACAPseq dataset.
source: Among baits that were listed in these databases and tested in the present study (47 for BioGRID and 43 for IntAct), there were only eight bait-target pairs in common between each database and the ACAPseq dataset (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The Results section provides quantitative comparison with IntAct shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The low degree of overlap between ACAPseq and public databases likely reflects incomplete coverage of published data in the public databases and the present lack of validation for many bait-target pairs.
source: This low degree of overlap (both in absolute numbers and relative to the total number of supra-threshold bait-target pairs) likely reflects (1) the incomplete coverage of published data in the public databases, and (2) the present lack of validation for many bait-target pairs.
evidence: The Results section provides an interpretation of the database comparison.

claim: ACAPseq detects interactions between FLRT1 and UNC5A and C.
source: ACAPseq detects interactions between FLRT1 and UNC5A and C, and between FLRT3 and UNC5A, B, C, and D (Supplemental file 1).
evidence: The Results section describes ACAPseq detection of FLRT-UNC5 interactions.

claim: ACAPseq detects interactions between FLRT3 and UNC5A, B, C, and D.
source: ACAPseq detects interactions between FLRT1 and UNC5A and C, and between FLRT3 and UNC5A, B, C, and D (Supplemental file 1).
evidence: The Results section describes ACAPseq detection of FLRT-UNC5 interactions.

claim: Pcdh9 mRNA shows approximately 100-fold higher ratio of PCDH9-Fc vs. EFNA1-Fc capture compared to other cadherin and protocadherin family members.
source: Pcdh9 mRNA shows a ~ 100 fold higher ratio of PCDH9-Fc vs. EFNA1-Fc capture compared to other cadherin and protocadherin family members.
evidence: The Results section describes the specificity of PCDH9 capture shown in Figure 6.

claim: Captured Pcdh9 mRNA shows approximately 100-fold enrichment over its starting mRNA abundance.
source: Captured Pcdh9 mRNA also shows a ~ 100 fold enrichment over its starting mRNA abundance.
evidence: The Results section describes the enrichment of Pcdh9 mRNA shown in Figure 6.

claim: None of the other cadherin or protocadherin mRNAs show more than several-fold enrichment over their starting abundances.
source: None of the other cadherin or protocadherin mRNAs show more than several-fold enrichment over their starting abundances, and the vast majority show either no change or a relative depletion following PCDH9-Fc capture.
evidence: The Results section describes the lack of enrichment for other cadherin/protocadherin family members shown in Figure 6.

claim: Pcdh9 mRNA is one of the more abundant cadherin/protocadherin mRNAs in neonatal mouse brain.
source: Figure 6B also shows that Pcdh9 mRNA is one of the more abundant cadherin/protocadherin mRNAs in neonatal mouse brain
evidence: The Results section describes the abundance of Pcdh9 mRNA shown in Figure 6B.

claim: PCDH9 interactions with cadherin/protocadherin family members in neonatal mouse brain are largely limited to homophilic binding.
source: If we assume that potential binding interactions between PCDH9 and other cadherin/protocadherin targets involve cadherin domains that are close to the amino-terminus and are therefore accessible in the context of the nascent polypeptide, then these data imply that PCDH9 interactions with cadherin/protocadherin family members in the neonatal mouse brain are largely limited to homophilic binding.
evidence: The Results section provides an interpretation of the PCDH9 specificity data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Fc-VEGF gave consistently higher capture efficiencies for Flt1, Kdr, and Nrp1 compared to VEGF-Fc in two independent experiments.
source: In each of two independent experiments, Fc-VEGF gave consistently higher capture efficiencies for Flt1, Kdr, and Nrp1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The Results section describes comparison of VEGF fusion configurations shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: VEGF-Fc produced no enrichment of Nrp1 polyribosomes over the starting polyribosome sample.
source: For Nrp1 polyribosomes, VEGF-Fc produced no enrichment over the starting polyribosome sample.
evidence: The Results section describes the lack of Nrp1 capture by VEGF-Fc shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The VEGF fusion configuration data emphasize the utility of exploring different configurations of bait-partner protein fusions when designing ACAPseq probes.
source: These data emphasize the utility of exploring different configurations of bait-partner protein fusions when designing ACAPseq probes.
evidence: The Results section provides an interpretation of the VEGF fusion configuration data.

claim: Approximately 16,000 (~70%) of protein-coding genes are expressed in testis.
source: RNAseq data indicate that ~ 16,000 (~70%) of protein-coding genes are expressed in testis, most likely as a consequence of a genome-wide process that resets the chromatin landscape (Soumillon et al., 2013).
evidence: The Results section cites published literature about testis transcriptome complexity.

claim: The high complexity of the testis transcriptome is most likely a consequence of a genome-wide process that resets the chromatin landscape.
source: RNAseq data indicate that ~ 16,000 (~70%) of protein-coding genes are expressed in testis, most likely as a consequence of a genome-wide process that resets the chromatin landscape (Soumillon et al., 2013).
evidence: The Results section cites published literature about the mechanism of testis transcriptome complexity.

claim: EFNA1-Fc captured multiple Epha targets with a high signal-to-noise ratio when incubated with adult mouse testis polyribosomes.
source: When EFNA1-Fc was incubated with adult mouse testis polyribosomes, multiple Epha targets were captured with a high signal-to-noise ratio (Figure 7A)
evidence: The Results section describes testis ACAPseq results shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Most Epha targets are present at more than 10-fold lower abundance in testis compared to brain.
source: even though most of the Epha targets are present at >10 fold lower abundance in testis compared to brain (Figure 7B).
evidence: The Results section describes the relative abundance of Epha targets in testis vs. brain shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Seven of eight Epha targets enriched in brain ACAPseq were observed to be enriched above the bulk of transcripts in testis ACAPseq.
source: By plotting the ratio of captured vs. starting RNA abundances, 7/8 Epha targets enriched in brain ACAPseq were observed to be enriched above the bulk of the transcripts in testis ACAPseq, with good agreement between the normalized brain and testis capture efficiencies (Figure 7D).
evidence: The Results section describes the comparison of brain and testis ACAPseq shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Epha6 is not detectably enriched in the testis ACAPseq sample.
source: The only exception to this pattern was Epha6, which is not detectably enriched in the testis sample.
evidence: The Results section describes the exception to the enrichment pattern shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Testis polyribosomes could serve as a useful starting material for ACAPseq.
source: These data suggest that testis polyribosomes could serve as a useful starting material for ACAPseq.
evidence: The Results section provides an interpretation of the testis ACAPseq data.

claim: The Cntn4 gene has alternative splicing that generates short and long protein isoforms.
source: Figure 8A and B shows an example of alternative splicing in the Cntn4 gene, in which inclusion of an alternate exon generates a short protein isoform that is missing the three carboxy-terminal fibronectin domains (GenBank NM_173004; available at https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/nuccore/NM_173004); skipping the alternate exon generates a long isoform that encodes the full-length protein (GenBank NM_001109749; available at https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/nuccore/NM_001109749.1).
evidence: The Results section describes alternative splicing in Cntn4 shown in Figure 8A and B.

claim: Both CNTN4 isoforms code for a protein that includes the PTPRG binding site in the second and third immunoglobulin domains.
source: Both isoforms code for a protein that includes the previously defined PTPRG binding site in the second and third immunoglobulin domains (Nikolaienko et al., 2016).
evidence: The Results section cites published literature about the PTPRG binding site in CNTN4.

claim: PTPRG-Fc captured transcripts corresponding to both long and short CNTN4 isoforms.
source: Using a PTPRG-Fc bait, transcripts corresponding to both long and short isoforms were captured by ACAPseq (Figure 8E).
evidence: The Results section describes capture of both CNTN4 isoforms shown in Figure 8E.

claim: The short CNTN4 isoform includes only eight amino acids that are not present in the long isoform.
source: We note that the short isoform includes only eight amino acids that are not present in the long isoform, which could make its detection by mass spectrometry challenging.
evidence: The Results section describes the structural difference between CNTN4 isoforms.

claim: EFNA1-Fc captured transcripts corresponding to both long and short EPHA7 isoforms.
source: An analogous result was obtained with ENA1-Fc capture of transcripts coding for long and short isoforms of EPHA7 (GenBank NM_010141 and NM_001122889, respectively).
evidence: The Results section describes capture of both EPHA7 isoforms shown in Figure 8F.

claim: Both EPHA7 isoforms contain the entire extracellular domain.
source: Both isoforms contain the entire ECD, but the short isoform is missing the cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase domain (Figure 8C,D and F).
evidence: The Results section describes the structural features of EPHA7 isoforms shown in Figure 8C, D, and F.

claim: The short EPHA7 isoform is missing the cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase domain.
source: Both isoforms contain the entire ECD, but the short isoform is missing the cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase domain (Figure 8C,D and F).
evidence: The Results section describes the structural features of EPHA7 isoforms shown in Figure 8C, D, and F.

claim: The region encompassing the trimerization domain and the three tandem EGF domains of TNR is essential for LRTM2-Fc binding.
source: This experiment shows that the region encompassing the trimerization domain and the three tandem EGF domains is essential for LRTM2-Fc binding.
evidence: The Results section describes the TNR deletion analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: LYPD6-AP bound to cells expressing CELSR1 and CELSR2, but not to cells expressing CELSR3.
source: As seen in Figure 8—figure supplement 2B, LYPD6-AP bound to cells expressing CELSR1 and CELSR2, but not to cells expressing CELSR3, consistent with the specificity seen in ACAPseq (Figure 2I–K and Figure 4G).
evidence: The Results section describes the LYPD6-CELSR binding assay shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The LYPD6-CELSR binding specificity observed in the cell binding assay is consistent with the specificity seen in ACAPseq.
source: As seen in Figure 8—figure supplement 2B, LYPD6-AP bound to cells expressing CELSR1 and CELSR2, but not to cells expressing CELSR3, consistent with the specificity seen in ACAPseq (Figure 2I–K and Figure 4G).
evidence: The Results section compares the cell binding assay results with ACAPseq results.

claim: PCDH19 demonstrates a distinctive mode of anti-parallel homophilic binding via an extended linear arrangement.
source: A structural analysis of the four amino-terminal cadherin domains of PCDH19, a non-clustered protocadherin, has demonstrated a distinctive mode of anti-parallel homophilic binding via an extended linear arrangement, with domains 1, 2, 3, and 4 of one monomer contacting domains 4, 3, 2, and 1, respectively, of the second monomer (Cooper et al., 2016).
evidence: The Results section cites published literature about PCDH19 structure.

claim: Clustered protocadherins exhibit a nearly identical mode of dimerization to PCDH19.
source: A nearly identical mode of dimerization is observed among clustered protocadherins (Goodman et al., 2016a; Goodman et al., 2016b; Nicoludis et al., 2016).
evidence: The Results section cites published literature about clustered protocadherin structure.

claim: N-cadherin has a homophilic binding affinity of approximately 20 μM.
source: consistent with the relatively low affinities characteristic of cadherin and proto-cadherin homophilic binding (e.g. ~20 μM and ~160 μM for N- and E-cadherin, respectively; Katsamba et al., 2009).
evidence: The Results section cites published literature about cadherin binding affinities.

claim: E-cadherin has a homophilic binding affinity of approximately 160 μM.
source: consistent with the relatively low affinities characteristic of cadherin and proto-cadherin homophilic binding (e.g. ~20 μM and ~160 μM for N- and E-cadherin, respectively; Katsamba et al., 2009).
evidence: The Results section cites published literature about cadherin binding affinities.

claim: Robust homophilic binding was observed with the full PCDH9 extracellular domain using magnetic bead aggregation assay.
source: Using aggregation of PCDH9-Fc coated Protein-G magnetic beads, an assay with higher avidity, we observed robust homophilic binding with the full ECD and with deletion derivatives lacking cadherin domains 5, 6, and 7, either singly or in combination (Figure 9A–C
evidence: The Results section describes the bead aggregation assay results shown in Figure 9A-C.

claim: Deletion of PCDH9 cadherin domains 1 or 4 dramatically reduced bead aggregation.
source: Deletion of cadherin domains 1 or 4 dramatically reduced bead aggregation.
evidence: The Results section describes the effects of domain deletions on bead aggregation shown in Figure 9.

claim: Deletion of PCDH9 cadherin domains 2 or 3 led to only a modest decrement in bead aggregation.
source: In contrast, deletion of cadherin domains 2 or 3 led to only a modest decrement in bead aggregation.
evidence: The Results section describes the effects of domain deletions on bead aggregation shown in Figure 9.

claim: Strong and specific aggregation was observed when one set of beads was coated with a deletion of PCDH9 cadherin domain 1 and the second set was coated with a deletion of cadherin domain 4.
source: Using LYPD6-Fc as a negative control, we observed strong and specific aggregation if one set of beads was coated with a deletion of cadherin domain one and the second set of beads was coated with a deletion of cadherin domain 4.
evidence: The Results section describes the mixed bead aggregation assay results shown in Figure 9D and E.

claim: Substantial aggregation was observed when one set of beads was coated with a deletion of PCDH9 cadherin domain 2 and the second set was coated with a deletion of cadherin domain 3.
source: Substantial aggregation was also observed if one set of beads was coated with a deletion of cadherin domain two and the second set of beads was coated with a deletion of cadherin domain 3.
evidence: The Results section describes the mixed bead aggregation assay results shown in Figure 9D and E.

claim: The bead aggregation data support an extended mode of anti-parallel homophilic binding for PCDH9 in which domains 1-4 are arranged in the same manner as for PCDH19 and clustered protocadherins.
source: Taken together, these data support an extended mode of anti-parallel homophilic binding for PCDH9 in which domains 1 – 4 are arranged in the same manner as for PCDH19 and the clustered protocadherins (Figure 9F).
evidence: The Results section provides an interpretation of the bead aggregation data shown in Figure 9F.

claim: Interactions between PCDH9 domains 1 and 4 may contribute more significantly to binding affinity than the interactions between domains 2 and 3.
source: As summarized in Figure 9G, in the context of this model, derivatives lacking either domains 2 or 3 are able to form a reasonably stable anti-parallel complex, suggesting that interactions between domains 1 and 4 may contribute more significantly to binding affinity than the interactions between domains 2 and 3.
evidence: The Results section provides an interpretation of the bead aggregation data shown in Figure 9G.

claim: ACAPseq interrogates the entire repertoire of translated proteins from the tissue of interest, including all splice isoforms, in a single reaction.
source: First, ACAPseq interrogates the entire repertoire of translated proteins from the tissue of interest, including all splice isoforms, in a single reaction.
evidence: The Discussion section describes an advantage of ACAPseq.

claim: ACAPseq is extremely sensitive, with starting abundance of target mRNAs as low as one part in 100,000.
source: Second, ACAPseq is extremely sensitive. Starting with 40 ug of polyribosome input, the starting abundance of target mRNAs can be as low as one part in 100,000 (~10 pg mRNA; for example Celsr1 and Flt1).
evidence: The Discussion section describes the sensitivity of ACAPseq.

claim: For rare mRNAs at one part in 100,000 abundance, the amount of specific mRNA captured is approximately 1 pg.
source: For such rare mRNAs, the amount of specific mRNA captured is ~1 pg.
evidence: The Discussion section provides quantitative data on capture amounts.

claim: Even a modest enrichment of 20-40 fold of RNAseq reads in the bait of interest vs. control baits provides a signal substantially above background.
source: Third, even a modest enrichment (e.g. 20–40 fold) of RNAseq reads in the bait of interest vs. control baits provides a signal that is substantially above background.
evidence: The Discussion section describes the signal-to-noise characteristics of ACAPseq.

claim: Polyribosome capture in ACAPseq depends on binding but not on biological function.
source: Fourth, polyribosome capture depends on binding but not on biological function.
evidence: The Discussion section describes an advantage of ACAPseq.

claim: The high valency of bait-coated magnetic beads and the poly-valent nature of polyribosomes suggest that relatively weak interactions can be detected by ACAPseq.
source: Fifth, the high valency of the bait-coated magnetic beads and the poly-valent nature of the polyribosome suggest that relatively weak interactions can be detected.
evidence: The Discussion section describes an advantage of ACAPseq.

claim: ACAPseq surveys protein products representing the full range of mRNA transcript diversity in the starting polyribosome population.
source: Sixth, ACAPseq surveys protein products representing the full range of mRNA transcript diversity in the starting polyribosome population.
evidence: The Discussion section describes an advantage of ACAPseq.

claim: False positives in ACAPseq could reflect interactions with unfolded or partially folded polypeptide targets.
source: First, false positives could reflect interactions with unfolded or partially folded polypeptide targets that might normally be resolved in vivo by chaperones or by interactions with bone fide binding partners but that persist in vitro under ACAPseq binding conditions.
evidence: The Discussion section provides a potential explanation for false positives.

claim: False positives in ACAPseq could reflect adventitious interactions between proteins that are spatially sequestered in vivo.
source: Second, false positives could reflect adventitious interactions between proteins that are spatially sequestered in vivo, for example between a secreted protein bait and a cytoplasmic protein target.
evidence: The Discussion section provides a potential explanation for false positives.

claim: False positives in ACAPseq could arise from non-optimal setting and/or weighting of threshold parameters.
source: Third, false positives could arise from a non-optimal setting and/or weighting of threshold parameters.
evidence: The Discussion section provides a potential explanation for false positives.

claim: Some baits may not have a polypeptide binding partner, making the negative finding a true negative.
source: First, some of the baits may not have a polypeptide binding partner – that is, the negative finding is a true negative.
evidence: The Discussion section provides a potential explanation for false negatives.

claim: The binding partner might not be expressed at high enough levels for its mRNA to be detected in ACAPseq.
source: Second, the binding partner might not be expressed at high enough levels (or at all) for its mRNA to be detected.
evidence: The Discussion section provides a potential explanation for false negatives.

claim: The configuration of the bait-Fc fusion protein may not allow bait-target binding.
source: Third, the configuration of the bait-Fc fusion protein may not allow bait-target binding, as seen in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 for VEGF-Fc and NRP1.
evidence: The Discussion section provides a potential explanation for false negatives with supporting data.

claim: The critical binding domain(s) in the target protein might not be correctly folded in the context of the nascent polypeptide.
source: Fourth, the critical binding domain(s) in the target protein might not be correctly folded in the context of the nascent polypeptide.
evidence: The Discussion section provides a potential explanation for false negatives.

claim: Studies of several multi-domain proteins have revealed native folding of individual domains while nascent polypeptides are still associated with the ribosome.
source: Studies of several artificial and natural multi-domain proteins have revealed native folding of individual domains while the nascent polypeptides are still associated with the ribosome (Chen et al., 1995; Han et al., 2012; Holtkamp et al., 2015)
evidence: The Discussion section cites published literature about nascent polypeptide folding.

claim: Binding could require co-assembly of two or more polypeptides or post-translational modifications that do not occur efficiently in the context of the nascent polypeptide.
source: Fifth, binding could require co-assembly of two or more polypeptides or could require post-translational modifications that do not occur (or do not occur efficiently) in the context of the nascent polypeptide.
evidence: The Discussion section provides a potential explanation for false negatives.

claim: Post-translational modifications that occur in the Golgi apparatus would be absent from polyribosome-bound nascent polypeptides derived from the rough endoplasmic reticulum.
source: For example, post-translational modifications that occur in the Golgi apparatus would be absent from polyribosome-bound nascent polypeptides, which are derived from the rough endoplasmic reticulum.
evidence: The Discussion section provides an explanation based on cell biology.

claim: A PPI could occur with a domain of the target protein that is too close to the carboxy-terminus for efficient binding when the nascent polypeptide is bound to the ribosome.
source: Sixth, a PPI could occur with a domain of the target protein that is too close to the carboxy-terminus for efficient binding when the nascent polypeptide is bound to the ribosome.
evidence: The Discussion section provides a potential explanation for false negatives.

claim: Many cell-surface proteins are oriented with their amino-termini facing the extracellular space (type one topology), which is the optimal arrangement for capturing their nascent polypeptides with ECD baits.
source: Conveniently, many cell-surface proteins are oriented with their amino-termini facing the extracellular space (type one topology; for example tyrosine kinase receptors), and this is the optimal arrangement for capturing their nascent polypeptides with ECD baits, as used here.
evidence: The Discussion section describes a favorable feature of cell-surface protein topology for ACAPseq.

claim: The ACAPseq signal may be too small to rise above the noise of non-specific interactions.
source: Seventh, the ACAPseq signal may be too small to rise above the noise of non-specific interactions.
evidence: The Discussion section provides a potential explanation for false negatives.

claim: Modifications to the ACAPseq protocol to reduce non-specific sticking and enhance reproducibility could reveal both lower affinity interactions and lower abundance mRNAs.
source: This last point can be appreciated by assessing the signal-to-noise ratio in the ASPs in Figure 4, and it suggests that modifications to the protocol to reduce non-specific sticking and enhance reproducibility of polyribosome capture could reveal both lower affinity interactions and lower abundance mRNAs.
evidence: The Discussion section provides a suggestion for improving ACAPseq.

claim: Adding chaperones or modifying enzymes to the polyribosome sample might improve ACAPseq performance.
source: The possibility that bait binding to nascent polypeptides might be limited by protein folding efficiency or post-translational modifications suggests that the addition of chaperones or modifying enzymes to the polyribosome sample might improve ACAPseq performance.
evidence: The Discussion section provides a suggestion for improving ACAPseq.

claim: Removing chaperones from polyribosomes might improve ACAPseq performance if chaperone-polypeptide complexes occlude access by the bait to adjacent folded domains.
source: Alternately, if unfolded or incompletely folded domains in nascent polypeptides are bound to chaperones and if the chaperone-polypeptide complex occludes access by the bait to adjacent folded domains, then removing chaperones from the polyribosomes might improve ACAPseq performance.
evidence: The Discussion section provides an alternative suggestion for improving ACAPseq.

claim: ACAPseq may be especially suitable for PPI discovery in organisms without extensive cDNA clone collections.
source: ACAPseq may be especially suitable for PPI discovery in these organisms because the nascent polypeptides displayed on polyribosomes present a target pool that approximates the complexity of the entire proteome.
evidence: The Discussion section describes a potential application of ACAPseq.

claim: ACAPseq is a novel PPI discovery platform that could complement existing PPI discovery platforms.
source: In sum, ACAPseq is a novel PPI discovery platform that could complement existing PPI discovery platforms.
evidence: The Discussion section provides a concluding statement about ACAPseq.

claim: All mice were housed and handled according to approved IACUC protocol MO16M367 of Johns Hopkins Medical Institutions.
source: All mice were housed and handled according to the approved Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) protocol MO16M367 of the Johns Hopkins Medical Institutions.
evidence: The Materials and methods section describes the ethical approval for animal use.
